title: The published npm page advertises 0.6.0 on every release since: README's version claims are outside the release procedure entirely
description:
Reported by opum-agent 2026-09-15 17:35Z, found first by lore-cli in its own package (LCLI-510, a recurrence of LCLI-325). `npm view @opum-ai/quest@0.7.1 readme` line 16 says "Published on npm as @opum-ai/quest@0.6.0" and line 23 says "Status: 0.6.0 released." README.md is in package.json files (line 33), so the registry serves it permanently for that version, and quest is a public package: this is what a stranger evaluating the CLI reads.

THE REPORTED DIAGNOSIS DOES NOT HOLD HERE, and the difference changes the fix. lore-cli diagnosed ORDERING -- a past-tense claim cannot be written before the release exists, so it is written after the tag, and each tag therefore carries the previous version README. That predicts dev is current and the tag lags by exactly one. Measured here instead: `git log -- README.md` returns ONE commit ever, a9fbc78, the post-recreation initial commit of 2026-09-10; and the status line reads "0.6.0 released" identically at v0.6.0, v0.6.2, v0.7.0, v0.7.1 AND on origin/dev right now. Nothing lags by one. The line is not written late -- it is not written at all. It was correct once, at 0.6.0, and no release since has looked at it.

So a hand-edit to 0.7.1 fixes this instance and nothing else, exactly as the reporter warned, but for a different reason than they gave: not because the ordering forces a stale tag, but because no step in the release procedure reads this file. Whichever cause, the repair is a mechanism.

WHY NOTHING CAUGHT IT: scripts/check-package-artifacts.mjs already asserts the tarball CONTAINS README.md (line 88) and says nothing about what is in it. A gate that looks at the file exists and can be taught the content claim.

NOT FIXABLE BY REPUBLISHING: those version pages are immutable. Any fix is only observable on the next publish, so the proof has to be planned as a pre-publish assertion plus a post-publish read, not a "the file looks right" check.

acceptanceCriteria.text: README.md carries no claim that can go stale without a release step noticing: either the version is generated at pack time from package.json, or the claim is made tense- and version-neutral and the specific numbers live where they are already maintained

A gate fails the release when README.md version claims disagree with package.json version -- extending scripts/check-package-artifacts.mjs, which today asserts only that README.md is present in the tarball
The gate is proven twice: red against a deliberately mismatched README, green on a clean tree, as two separate runs with the exit code and message read from each log

Post-publish verification is written into the release procedure as a step, landing in scripts/qualification/ beside the receipt verifier rather than inline in release.yml (inline read-back logic is unreachable by any test, which is how two defects survived a fully green run on lore-cli PR #118). It must read the per-version README out of the published TARBALL -- npm pack @opum-ai/quest@<new>, or the registry tarball URL -- and re-run the pre-publish assertions over those bytes, so the check cannot drift from the generator. It must NOT use npm view @opum-ai/quest@<new> readme: that field is packument-level, measured inert across 0.7.1/0.6.2/0.6.0 (identical 8387 bytes, same sha256), so it cannot distinguish versions and can never make this assertion. Criterion text amended 2026-09-15; the original named the npm view probe. The fix stays unobservable until the next publish.
Coordinated with lore-cli so the fix is one mechanism or two deliberately-separate ones, not two accidental ones -- they hold the earlier instance (LCLI-325) and the recurrence (LCLI-510)

implementationNotes:
MECHANISM SETTLED WITH lore-cli 2026-09-15: option (b), two implementations against one written contract, NOT one shared check. Reasoning on both sides: the shared-check option (a) needs a home, and neither repo owns shared tooling, so it would make one CLI a consumer of its siblings release machinery -- a permanent coupling to buy a check of roughly twenty lines. Quest has the cheaper half already: scripts/check-package-artifacts.mjs:88 asserts the tarball CONTAINS README.md and says nothing about its content, so this extends an existing gate that already runs in the release path.

WHY THE CONTRACT IS PHRASED AS ASSERTIONS AND NOT AS A PROCEDURE: lore cause is ordering (tag, then the README bump lands on dev after), quest cause is that the line is outside the release procedure entirely. A procedural contract -- "bump the README before tagging" -- fixes lore and does nothing here, because there is no bump step to reorder. An assertion contract fixes both.

lore-cli drafted five assertions and quest agreed them with three refinements:
A1 the gate reads the PACKED artifact, not the working tree -- refined to "each published package that ships a README", because quest publishes seven packages and only the wrapper carries one (package.json files is bin/quest.cjs, README.md, LICENSE; platform packages are built with files: [bin/<executable>] at build-platform-packages.mjs:86).
A2 a shipped README may not assert its own released version in any form that can go stale -- including when it is currently correct, because correctness at one moment is what makes it invisible at the next. Taken verbatim.
A3 the release REFUSES rather than warns on disagreement -- refined, because as drafted it names no testable object. Proposed: the version-bearing lines occupy a MARKED REGION; the release asserts the region is present, its content equals byte-for-byte what the generator produces for package.json version, and no occurrence of the package own name adjacent to a version appears outside it. Measured argument for the scoping rule: grep -oE for semver in this README returns 4 tokens, all 0.6.0, so a naive any-semver matcher runs clean HERE TODAY with zero false positives -- which is exactly the condition under which the scoping rule looks unnecessary and then is not, the first time the README cites a Node floor or a historical version. The byte-equality clause also gives A3 a second job: catching a broken GENERATOR, not only a stale hand-edit.
A4 post-publish read-back is a CONFIRMATION and explicitly not the gate, because published version pages are immutable so it can only observe the defect, never prevent it -- refined to record the package and version read back, not only the verdict.
A5 each implementation records which assertions it enforces and where, so an enforced assertion is distinguishable from an aspired one without reading two release scripts.

lore-cli will propose the folded text to opum-doc rather than landing it there. Implementation here waits on that text.

IMPLEMENTED. Took A2 "absent" arm rather than the generated one: README.md now states no version of its own. Measured after: zero version-shaped tokens in the file. The number lives in package.json, the tags and the npm page, all maintained already, and the npm page shows it above the README anyway -- so the prose restatement bought nothing and cost a permanent wrong advertisement on two published versions.

opum-doc ODOC-201 finding verified rather than taken, and it is slightly stronger than they stated: THREE lines carried a stale version (16, 23, 25), across two prose sites -- the "Published on npm as" bullet, and the Status blockquote which asserts the version twice within itself. Marking only the Status LINE would have left line 25 stale as well as line 16.

A GAP IN THE CONTRACT I SIGNED OFF, found at implementation. A3 clause 3 as agreed scopes to "the package own name adjacent to a version". The worst site here -- `**Status: 0.6.0 released.**` -- carries the version on a line with NO package name on it; the nearest package name is on the next line. So clause 3 as written would not have caught the very defect it was added for. Quest therefore enforces a STRONGER form: no version-shaped token anywhere in the packed README, outside an optional marked region. Zero false positives today, measured. lore-cli cannot use this form (nine legitimate version tokens in their README) and implements the scoped clause; the divergence is exactly what A5 exists to record. Reported to lore-cli and opum-doc.

ENFORCEMENT, in scripts/check-package-artifacts.mjs (A5 record is the docblock there):
A1 enforced -- the subject is README.md read back out of a REAL npm pack tarball, not the working tree. Subject set is declared not discovered: root files is a closed list, the six platform packages declare files: [bin/<executable>] and ship no README, and the pre-existing assertion fails if either changes.
A2 enforced, absent arm.
A3 enforced, stronger form, with marker support present so adding a legitimate version later is a deliberate visible act rather than a silent loosening of the matcher.
A4 NOT enforced here and cannot be -- immutable version pages mean the read-back can only observe, never prevent. It belongs to the release procedure; criterion 4 stays open.

PROOF, three runs, every exit code read unpiped:
  clean tree                                    exit 0
  Status-line defect reintroduced verbatim      exit 1, names the version and the immutability
  package-name-adjacent bullet defect           exit 1
  restored clean tree                           exit 0
Full suite: bun run check exit 0, 506 pass 0 fail across 58 files. lore check 0 errors.

PR #132 merged into dev as 0c3117f. Required checks on head e55ce88: source-gates SUCCESS (twice; the push trigger fires because this is a genuine source change, so the double fire is correct here rather than the diagnostic signal it was on PR #131), Tracker integrity SUCCESS, lore check SUCCESS.

CRITERION 4 IS THE ONLY ONE OPEN and it is deliberately not delivered here. It asks for the post-publish read-back to be written into the release procedure, which means editing scripts/publish-release.mjs. The hazard is specific and already documented in that file: it carries a retry loop added because a read-back ran seconds after a successful publish, hit CDN propagation lag, and marked a completed release as failed -- its own comment says "a red run on a successful publish is how a real failure gets ignored later". A second read-back without equivalent propagation handling reintroduces exactly that. It is a small change that belongs to a session doing release work with a publish it can observe, not to one bolting it on with nothing to publish against.

Nothing blocks on it: dev carries no version bump, and the token rotation is deferred by user ruling on QCLI-308, so there is no release waiting. Parking rather than leaving the task In Progress unattended.

A5 record extended with what lore-cli enforces, reported 2026-09-15, and marked as their DECISION rather than their proof -- they stated explicitly that they are implementing now and that "proven" is pending exit codes. Recorded in scripts/check-package-artifacts.mjs so this side A5 entry is not half a picture.

Their predicate is block-scoped name-plus-version adjacency, where a block is a maximal run of lines delimited by a blank line or a bare ">", with region lines excised before evaluation. That is the clause that separates it from the landed floor: on both READMEs the stale Status: line and the package-name line sit in one blockquote paragraph, so a line matcher passes and a block matcher fires.

They diverge from quest in a second way worth recording: TWO marked regions, not one, because their stale sites are not contiguous and a single spanning region would swallow a paragraph of legitimate historical version citations that no generator could reproduce from package.json without fabricating them. Quest code supports exactly one marker pair, so a future need for a second here is a code change rather than a README change -- noted in the docblock as a code fact, not a policy one.

They also cite an ODOC-203 amendment stating lore is the only side that will ever exercise A3 clause 2. Taken secondhand; not read here, and the docblock attributes it to their report rather than asserting it.

THREE follow-ups from lore-cli 2026-09-15, all acted on.

1. LORE A5 LINES UPGRADED FROM DECIDED TO PROVEN, with the evidence they sent: lore-cli PR #118, CI run 35016083790 on a390713c, resolved with lore 0.7.0 / quest 0.7.1 / Bun 1.3.14 / Node 24.20.0. Recorded their mutation matrix rather than only their pass count -- line-scoped clause 3 fails 2, exempting a block overlapping a region fails 2, line-wise region excision fails 1, disabling byte-equality fails 5, deleting the gate fails 1, unmutated 0 of 20. The matrix is the part worth trusting: it measures that each clause is load-bearing rather than that the suite is green.

2. ODOC-203 NOW CITED FIRST-HAND, at their request rather than left as their relay. Read via the API at opum-doc main@b596ca5: the table marks lore "yes -- the only side that does" for A3 byte-equality and quest "no -- vacuous by construction", and the document additionally REQUIRES a vacuous clause to carry its reason, because "vacuous because there is no generator to break" and "vacuous because nobody implemented it" are the same word for opposite situations. Their relay was accurate in every clause; verifying it cost one call and removes a hypothesis from the record.

3. REGION AMBIGUITY REFUSAL PORTED from their locateRegions. Worth being precise about what it fixed, because my first reading of their warning was wrong: they said a second marker pair would make quest silently swallow everything between the first opener and the last closer. It would not -- this code takes indexOf for BOTH markers, so a second region falls outside the first and trips the stray-version check, failing loudly. But it fails with the WRONG DIAGNOSIS, reporting a version "outside a version-claim region" when the version is in fact inside the second one. A correct refusal with a misleading message is the expensive kind to debug, so the port earns its place for a different reason than the one offered. Also added an out-of-order marker check.

NEW PROOFS, four shapes, exit codes read unpiped:
  two marker pairs                exit 1, names the counts and says the extent is ambiguous
  one region stating 0.7.1        exit 0
  one region stating 0.0.1        exit 1, "region does not state 0.7.1"
  unbalanced markers              exit 1
  restored clean tree             exit 0
The second of those is the one that had never been run: every earlier proof exercised the REJECT path, and nothing had ever demonstrated that the marked region -- the escape hatch the docblock tells a future editor to reach for -- actually works. Prove it accepts as well as rejects, applied to the escape hatch rather than to the gate.

4. THEIR FIXTURE TRAP DOES NOT EXIST HERE, checked rather than assumed. Their publish-release.sh suite stubbed a plain text file as a root tarball, so the new gate could not gunzip it and 11 tests failed as "could not read" -- indistinguishable from the gate working. Quest gate consumes no fixture; it runs a real npm pack. The one adjacent thing is scripts/test-package-artifact-delivery.mjs:45, which stubs check:packages as a no-op -- deliberate, because that suite tests delivery ORDERING, and the real check runs in source-gates via prepublish.mjs:228, which is what caught the npm/quest-darwin-arm64 deletion earlier today.

Full suite: bun run check exit 0, 506 pass 0 fail, 4327 expect() calls across 58 files. lore check 0 errors.

CITATION WITHDRAWN, and the failure is mine as much as lore-cli.

07dcacb recorded lore A5 lines as PROVEN, citing "lore-cli PR #118, CI run 35016083790 on a390713c". lore-cli flagged that they sent that id while the run was still in_progress -- it was the ADDRESS of a proof, not a proof. Verified first-hand rather than taken: repos/opum-ai/lore-cli/actions/runs/35016083790 returns conclusion=failure, one failing job "lint · typecheck · test (windows-latest)", GNU tar on the Windows runner reading C:\... as a host:path remote spec. Their report was accurate in every clause.

MY HALF OF IT, which is the part worth keeping. The same commit re-resolved ODOC-203 first-hand at opum-doc main@b596ca5 SPECIFICALLY so the record would not carry a relay -- and then, in the adjacent paragraph, recorded a CI run id without opening it. The rule was applied to one citation and skipped on the other inside a single edit. An id is not a measurement; resolving it costs one API call. Nothing about having just articulated the rule prevented it, which is the same observation this repository CLAUDE.md already makes about claims that were true when written.

A5 lines are back to DECIDED AND LOCALLY MEASURED with an explicit instruction not to cite them as proven until a green run arrives. Their local measurements stand and are what the block records. Two of their matrix figures have already moved (the suite is 23 tests, not 20, and gains an inline-marker row), so the old numbers are marked superseded rather than repeated.

THEIR RENDERING DEFECT IS A LIVE TRAP FOR QUEST ESCAPE HATCH, and is now a refusal. A marker whose line CONTENT begins with <!-- opens a CommonMark HTML block that swallows the rest of the line as raw text -- so a marker written as "- <!-- ... -->" or "> <!-- ... -->" renders the surrounding prose literally on the npm page while every A3 clause passes. lore-cli found it with GitHub own POST /markdown on a page emitting a literal **Status: 0.7.0 released.**, asterisks and all. No version assertion can see it: the bytes are correct and only the rendering is wrong.

Quest has no markers today so it cannot be hit -- but the docblock INSTRUCTS a future editor to add one, and a list item or blockquote is exactly where a version claim lives. So this was a trap planted by my own documentation. Now refused at the moment it is introduced.

PROOFS, exit codes unpiped:
  marker opening a blockquote line          exit 1, names the line and the CommonMark cause
  marker anchored after prose on its line   exit 0
  restored clean tree                       exit 0
The second matters for the same reason the earlier region-acceptance proof did: a refusal that rejects every form of the sanctioned escape hatch is a broken escape hatch, and only the accept run distinguishes them.

FOR CRITERION 4, which is still open: lore-cli A4 was wrong in a way only a real publish would have revealed. It grepped the served README for a literal "**Status: <version> released.**" which no longer appears contiguously, because their own markers split it -- so it would have gone RED ON A CORRECT RELEASE, seconds after the irreversible step. Their fix is the shape quest criterion 4 should copy: write the served bytes beside the release package.json and re-run --check over them, so the assertion cannot drift from the generator because it IS the generator. A grep-based read-back is the wrong design and this is the second time a read-back has threatened to mark a good publish bad here -- the existing propagation retry loop in publish-release.mjs is the first.

Full suite: bun run check exit 0, 506 pass 0 fail across 58 files. lore check 0 errors.

lore-cli N+1 AUDIT TRANSLATED AND ANSWERED, plus three proofs that were missing.

Their setup: lore regions are declared in code, so an implementation silently specialised to the two that exist would pass their entire suite, because every other test exercises exactly those two. Their sharpest assertion is that a newly declared third region carries the package own name next to a version in its GENERATED content -- because a masking rule specialised to the known ids would make the gate refuse what its own generator produces. Mutation confirms it: restricting their region machinery to the first two ids fails all five of those tests and nothing else in their suite notices.

QUEST IS NOT EXPOSED TO THE SPECIALISATION, for a structural reason rather than a virtuous one: a second region here is an explicit refusal, not a silent first-match. Limited and loud rather than specialised and quiet. But the underlying question survives translation and was UNPROVEN here, so I ran it:

  G. region content carrying `@opum-ai/quest@0.7.1` and `v0.7.1`   exit 0
     -- the gate does NOT refuse what a generator would legitimately emit
  H1. stray 1.2.3 BEFORE the region                                exit 1, names 1.2.3
  H2. stray 4.5.6 AFTER the region                                 exit 1, names 4.5.6
  restored clean tree                                              exit 0

H1 and H2 matter because excision splices two slices around the region; a one-sided bug would mask strays on whichever side was dropped and nothing else would notice. G is the one their framing produced and I would not have written: every prior region proof used bare version text, so "does the exemption reject the exempt thing" had never been asked.

The general form, worth keeping apart from either repository answer: AN EXEMPTION MECHANISM MUST BE PROVED NOT TO REJECT THE EXEMPT THING, which is a different measurement from proving it rejects the unexempt thing. That is the accept/reject discipline applied to an exemption rather than to a gate.

CI STATUS RECORDED NARROWLY AND DELIBERATELY. lore-cli run 35017881343 on de319a1f is green on every job including lint · typecheck · test (windows-latest), which establishes that the GNU-tar failure behind the withdrawn citation is FIXED. It does NOT establish their implementation: they pushed 159f7d2d afterwards, so de319a1f is green and is no longer their head. They flagged that distinction themselves before anyone could record it. Recording "green run" and "green head" as one fact is how the first citation went wrong, in the other direction.

A CREDIT I GAVE THEM AND THEY CORRECTED, kept because the corrected version is the useful one. I said reaching for GitHub POST /markdown was the move worth stealing. They report they did not reach for it out of rigour -- they wanted to see whether the README still looked right, and expected confirmation. So the rule is not "render your markdown". It is: THE ARTIFACT A READER SEES IS A DIFFERENT OBJECT FROM THE ARTIFACT THE GATE READS, AND ONLY ONE OF THEM IS WHAT WAS PROMISED TO ANYONE. Their gate read README.md; the npm page is a rendering of it; nothing in this thread compared the two until an aesthetic impulse made someone look.

HANDOFF at session recycle, 2026-09-15. Session ending on context budget, not on a blocker. Nothing is In Progress (verified by `quest task list --status "In Progress"`, empty), the tree is clean and 0 commits are unpushed (verified by `git status --short` and `git rev-list --count @{u}..HEAD`), dev is at 44cc05e, and `quest doctor` reports healthy.

WHERE THIS TASK STANDS. A1, A2, A3 and A5 of the shipped-README contract are implemented and landed across PRs #131-#137. Criterion 4 is the ONLY open one and is deliberately unstarted, not forgotten.

WHAT CRITERION 4 NEEDS, and why it was not bolted on. It is the post-publish read-back, which means editing scripts/publish-release.mjs. Two independent reasons to do it with a real publish in hand rather than from a cold session:
  1. That script already carries a propagation retry loop, added after a read-back ran seconds past a successful publish, hit CDN lag, and marked a completed release as failed. Its own comment says "a red run on a successful publish is how a real failure gets ignored later".
  2. lore-cli hit the SAME class of defect from a different direction on their A4: their read-back grepped the served README for a literal "**Status: <version> released.**" which their own markers had split, so it would have gone red on a CORRECT release, seconds after the irreversible step.
So a grep-based read-back is the wrong design here, twice established. THE SHAPE TO COPY is lore-cli fix: write the served bytes beside the release package.json and re-run --check over them, so the assertion cannot drift from the generator because it IS the generator. A grep encodes the output format in a second place, which is the two-records-nobody-compares shape this whole contract exists to prevent.

UNVERIFIED BELIEF, flagged as one: I have not read lore-cli implementation of that fix, only their description of it.

WHAT THE NEXT SESSION SHOULD NOT REDO. The A5 block in scripts/check-package-artifacts.mjs cites NO CI run as proof of lore-cli side, on purpose. Their run 35017881343 on de319a1f is green including the Windows job, which establishes their GNU-tar fix and nothing more -- they pushed 159f7d2d after it, so that SHA is green and is no longer their head. Do not upgrade those lines to "proven" until lore-cli sends a green run on their CURRENT head with per-job confirmation; they said they would. A previous revision here (07dcacb) cited a FAILING run as proof and had to be withdrawn in #136.

SKILLS THE NEXT SESSION WILL WANT: opum-sdlc before any branch or PR, opum-handoff on restore, and `quest instructions task-execution` before moving this task off Paused.

OTHER OPEN WORK, all filed with full descriptions and criteria and needing no context from this session: QCLI-308 (publish credential inventory; rotation DEFERRED by this repository own user 2026-09-15, do not re-litigate, the guard in criterion 3 is independent of that ruling), QCLI-309 (codex skill-file write; an unblock sequence that works on 0.7.1 today is on the task and should reach mbpm2), QCLI-310 (--if-revision is workspace-wide, a correctness defect against its own help text), QCLI-311 (quest complete rename forces git add -A; both arms open, lore-cli registered no preference), QCLI-312 (no narrow read; --max-notes rejects 0, which is half a validator change).

LORE SIDE NOW QUALIFIED IN CI ON ITS TRUE HEAD, and my earlier unverified belief is closed. Supersedes the handoff note above on both points.

VERIFIED FIRST-HAND, every clause re-resolved through the API rather than taken from lore-cli report:
  opum-ai/lore-cli PR #118   state=open   headRefOid=930935d9bc37402ed18aae20b16f2f4c0754aa7e
  run 35018902430            completed    conclusion=success    headSha=930935d9bc...
  13 jobs: 11 success, 2 skipped -- "promotion is manual" and "main is fast-forward of dev", which run only on PRs into main and are not required contexts there
  lint · typecheck · test (windows-latest) = SUCCESS, closing the GNU-tar failure behind the withdrawn citation
The run headSha and the PR headRefOid are the SAME SHA. That identity is the entire claim and is exactly what could not be said about either earlier citation. Their report was accurate in every clause.

STILL NOT LANDED, and the record says so rather than rounding up. PR #118 is OPEN. The run qualifies the implementation; it does not put it on lore dev. A tracker-completion commit goes into their delivering PR, so the SHA may move while nothing about the implementation changes -- lore-cli flagged that themselves before anyone could record it wrong. Do not upgrade the A5 block to "landed" except against a run on their dev.

THE DISTINCTION HAS NOW FAILED THREE DISTINCT WAYS HERE, and the wording was what hid it every time. A FAILING run cited as proof (07dcacb, withdrawn in #136). A GREEN run on a SHA two commits behind the head (de319a1f, recorded narrowly). And now a green run on the true head of a branch that has not landed. All three read as "CI is green" in prose. The A5 block carries all three, because the useful artifact is the list of ways the sentence can be true and useless, not the current verdict.

MY UNVERIFIED BELIEF FROM THE HANDOFF NOTE IS NOW CLOSED, and it resolved in favour of the prescription. I had flagged that I read lore-cli DESCRIPTION of their A4 fix, not the implementation. They have since read their own implementation and confirm: .github/workflows/release.yml, publish job, step "Read the shipped README back off the registry, naming what was read (LCLI-510, A4)" writes the served bytes to a temp dir beside the release package.json and re-runs `node scripts/shipped-readme-version.mjs --check --dir "$workdir"`. The assertion IS the generator; no grep for a literal survives. That is still their reading of their own code rather than mine -- a smaller gap than before, and named rather than closed.

They also confirm the near miss was actual history rather than my reconstruction: the first version searched for "**Status: 0.7.0 released.**", which does not appear contiguously in what the registry serves because the source reads "**Status:<!--lore-version:status:begin--> 0.7.0 released.**". It would have gone red on a correct release, seconds after the one irreversible action. Their write-up keeps the honest part: neither half was caught by a test, because the A4 step only runs inside a real publish. That is the strongest argument on record for why THIS repository criterion 4 must be built with a real publish in hand -- an untestable step is exactly the one that cannot be proven cold.

CONTEXT CONSUMPTION THIS PASS, measured from this session own transcript rather than estimated, at the orchestrator request. lore-cli hypothesis was that the harness re-displays whole files after Bash/heredoc edits to files already in context. ANSWER: the mechanism is real here too, it fired, and it did NOT generalise as a significant consumer -- roughly 3 percent upper bound against 44 percent for something else entirely.

METHOD: parsed ~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session>.jsonl (3.16 MB on disk), bucketing content payloads by category. 487017 bytes of content counted; the gap to 3.16 MB is JSON envelope and metadata I did not count, so treat the percentages as shares of counted content, not of the file.

  my tool_use input (Bash)              213011   43.7%   171 calls
  tool_result (bash/gh/test output)     108752   22.3%   191
  my outbound SendMessage                79694   16.4%    17
  user/other text                        33843    6.9%     3
  INBOUND cross-session messages         27362    5.6%     7
  my assistant prose                     22569    4.6%    59

THE RESULT CONTRADICTS MY OWN GUESS, which is why it was worth measuring. I would have said inbound peer traffic dominated -- seven long messages from three sessions. It is 5.6 percent. About 65 percent of counted content is text I AUTHORED: Bash inputs, outbound messages, and prose. I consumed my context by writing, not by reading.

ON lore-cli HYPOTHESIS SPECIFICALLY: raw grep finds 2 re-display events ("changed on disk since you last read it" / "Here are the relevant changes"), in JSONL lines totalling 14442 bytes -- an UPPER BOUND, since a whole line carries other content too. Against 487017 counted, that is at most ~3 percent. Nine further events were one-line "modified ... you have previously read" notices totalling 2489 bytes, which are pointers, not dumps.

THE REFINEMENT WORTH MORE THAN THE VERDICT: both re-display events were on CLAUDE.md, which enters context at session start as project instructions and which the harness therefore holds IN FULL. My ~15 other heredoc edits -- to scripts/check-package-artifacts.mjs and README.md -- produced only one-line notices, because I never Read those files whole; I only ever viewed slices with `sed -n` and `grep`. So the hypothesis sharpens from "Bash/heredoc edits cause re-display" to: RE-DISPLAY FIRES FOR FILES THE HARNESS HOLDS IN FULL, NOT FOR FILES YOU HAVE ONLY SLICED. That is testable, and the mitigation follows from it -- do not Read whole a file you intend to heredoc-edit; slice it. I did that by accident, because auto-mode instructs Bash-first editing, not because I knew this.

WHAT ACTUALLY COST ME, and the lesson is not lore-cli: the top 10 of 171 Bash calls are 58232 bytes, 27 percent of all Bash input, and every one of them is a commit-message-plus-PR-body heredoc or a long quest note. A tracker note, a commit message and a PR body describing the same change means paying for that prose three times in one turn, in full, as tool input. Outbound SendMessage averaged 4.7 KB across 17 messages. Both are self-inflicted and both are the direct cost of the thoroughness this session was otherwise right to have -- so the trade is real, not a pure defect. 1. npm's readme IS A PACKUMENT-LEVEL FIELD, NOT A PER-VERSION PAGE -- VERIFIED AGAINST @opum-ai/quest RATHER THAN TAKEN FROM THEIR REPORT. The version qualifier is inert:
     npm view @opum-ai/quest@0.7.1 readme -> 8387 bytes, sha256 289b3523dc7fb760...

   THIS DISPROVES THE PROBE NAMED IN ACCEPTANCE CRITERION 4. Criterion 4 as filed reads "npm view @opum-ai/quest@<new> readme must agree with the published version". That command cannot distinguish versions, so it can never make that assertion -- it would pass or fail identically whatever was published. The criterion's INTENT survives untouched (post-publish read-back written into the release procedure); only its named mechanism is dead. Per-version README bytes have to come from the tarball -- npm pack @opum-ai/quest@<version>, or the registry tarball URL -- which is the same object scripts/check-package-artifacts.mjs already reads pre-publish, so the read-back can re-run the generator rather than grep, the shape lore-cli arrived at independently.

   Criterion 4's text is left as filed rather than rewritten: --acceptance-criteria replaces the whole list and takes a string array, so amending one entry would drop the four checked states on the others. This note is the amendment. Whoever implements criterion 4: do not reach for the probe the criterion names.

   Second-order consequence, because it changes what the ORIGINAL bug report measured, not just what the fix should do: the report cited "npm view @opum-ai/quest@0.7.1 readme line 16". That was reading the packument readme, not 0.7.1's page. CORRECTION TO THE PRECEDING NOTE, AND CRITERION 4 IS NOW AMENDED IN PLACE.

The preceding note said criterion 4's text was left as filed because "--acceptance-criteria replaces the whole list and takes a string array, so amending one entry would drop the four checked states on the others." THE SECOND HALF OF THAT IS FALSE. The flag takes EITHER a string array OR an array of {index,text,checked} items, and the object form preserves everything. Criterion 4 has been amended; all four checked states survived, confirmed by reading the record back.

WHERE THE FALSE CLAIM CAME FROM, because it is the exact failure this repository's CLAUDE.md warns about and I walked into it anyway inside the same hour I recorded the warning: `quest manifest --json` describes the flag as `{"value":"json-array"}` and nothing more. I read that, inferred "array of strings", and wrote the inference down as a measurement. The object form appears in exactly one place in the CLI's own output -- the usage error you get for passing it wrong:

  --acceptance-criteria must be a JSON array of strings or {index,text,checked} items.

So the capability is documented only on the failure path. You cannot discover it by reading the manifest, and `quest help task edit`'s summary describes --check-ac/--uncheck-ac/--remove-ac and the position/index distinction at length without mentioning that --acceptance-criteria takes objects at all.

MEASURED, in a throwaway workspace rather than against a real task -- three criteria, positions 1 and 3 checked:
  string array, one text amended            both checked items SILENTLY reset to false
  objects without `index`                   exit 2 usage, and the message is what named the object form
  objects with {index,text,checked}         one text amended, both checked states preserved

The silent reset is the part worth carrying. Nothing warns; the envelope comes back kind=task.updated with the checkboxes cleared, and a caller who did not read the record back would not know. Filed separately as the product gap it is -- this is the CLI this repository owns, and the defect was found by using it, not by reading it.

WHAT THIS CHANGES ABOUT THE PRECEDING NOTE: only the parenthetical about why criterion 4 was left alone. Finding 1 (npm readme is packument-level, criterion 4's named probe disproven), finding 2 (the inline/extracted split of quest's post-publish read-backs) and finding 3 (the clause-3 probe, four runs, exit codes unpiped) were each measured and all three stand unchanged. The one clause I did not measure is the one that was wrong, which is the whole of the lesson.
